name: Low-dose isotretinoin (microdosing Accutane)

card.summary: Using small continuous isotretinoin (Accutane) amounts, instead of a standard course, to keep acne away with fewer side effects; discussed online, thinly documented here.
card.note: Isotretinoin is a prescription teratogen with a boxed psychiatric warning; regimens are set by a prescriber.

quick.overview:
Low-dose isotretinoin, often called microdosing Accutane online, refers to taking much smaller amounts of the prescription acne drug than a standard course, sometimes continuously, with the stated aim of keeping skin clear while reducing side effects.

On looksmax.org, users discuss whether a small maintenance amount after a full course could help results last, and some combine the idea with a topical retinoid [1]. The reference sources reviewed for this article describe isotretinoin's standard use and risks but give no low-dose study results [2].
quick.mechanism: Isotretinoin is described as the only acne drug affecting all four main processes in acne [2]. The rationale given by proponents is that a smaller exposure might preserve benefit with fewer dose-related effects; the sources reviewed here do not test that idea.
quick.risks: Isotretinoin is prescription-only in most countries, a known teratogen (US Pregnancy Category X) and subject to the iPLEDGE programme in the US. Common effects include dry lips, skin and eyes; psychiatric effects have been reported and the US label has carried a boxed warning since 2005 [2].

lead: Low-dose isotretinoin, popularly called microdosing Accutane, is the practice of taking markedly smaller doses of isotretinoin than the standard acne regimen, in some cases as an ongoing maintenance approach. Isotretinoin is a prescription retinoid first patented by Roche in 1969 and approved by the FDA in 1982 [2].

Within looksmaxxing forums the idea appears as a way to preserve clear skin after a conventional course finishes. A looksmax.org thread, for instance, asks whether a small maintenance amount after finishing a cycle would help acne stay away, and a respondent says it would, adding that a low-strength topical retinoid is sometimes paired with it [1]. These are individual user statements, not clinical findings.

The reference sources reviewed for this article do not report results for low-dose regimens. They do state that the dose may be lowered to reduce side effects and that psychiatric side-effect risk rises with dose [2]. The entry is therefore documented mainly as a community practice.

paras: The term covers a range of approaches in which isotretinoin is taken at a fraction of conventional dosing, either as a gentler primary treatment or as continued upkeep after a course. No single definition is used across forums, and doses are not specified here.

Isotretinoin was developed by Roche, patented in 1969 and approved by the FDA in 1982. Roche's patents expired in 2002, allowing generics, and the Accutane brand was discontinued in 2009, although overseas affiliates still market it as Roaccutane [2]. The wiki found no source documenting when or by whom the term microdosing Accutane was first popularised.

Forum users who discuss it say a small continuing amount acts as maintenance that keeps skin clear and prevents relapse. In one looksmax.org thread, a respondent describes it as a very low dose that would keep skin in good condition, and another user asks whether combining it with a topical retinoid would be a problem [1].

Reference sources describe standard isotretinoin courses as the most effective acne medication: after one course about 80 percent improve and over half achieve complete remission, with a second course bringing cumulative efficacy to about 96 percent [3]. They note dose may be lowered to reduce side effects, and that depression risk is reported as much higher at very high doses than at normal ones [2]. The sources reviewed do not contain trial results on low-dose or maintenance regimens.

Common effects of isotretinoin include dry lips, skin and eyes and sun sensitivity; liver effects require blood monitoring; psychiatric effects such as depression and anxiety are reported, with a US boxed warning since 2005 [2]. Some effects such as dry eye may persist after stopping [2]. The drug is a known teratogen, and since 2006 US dispensing has run through the iPLEDGE programme, which requires registration, pregnancy testing and contraception for patients who can become pregnant [2]. Whether lower doses change these risks is not addressed in the sources reviewed.
No studies found for low-dose isotretinoin in the sources reviewed. Standard-course isotretinoin is extensively studied, as summarised in reference works [2][3].

timeline.event: A boxed warning on psychiatric effects is in place in the US [2].
iPLEDGE replaces the earlier SMART programme in the US [2].

lore.intro: Low-dose Accutane is discussed on looksmax.org mainly as a possible way to keep results after a full course [1].

claims.claim: A tiny maintenance amount after a full course keeps acne from coming back
claims.believers: A thread starter on looksmax.org asks whether a small continuing amount after finishing a cycle would help keep the skin clear, and a respondent answers that it is a very low dose that maintains skin [1].
claims.experts: The reference sources reviewed describe standard-course outcomes and note that dose may be lowered to reduce side effects, but report no studies of long-term maintenance at low doses [2][3].

claims.claim: A low-dose oral retinoid and a low-strength topical retinoid can be used together
claims.believers: One user in the thread reports using the two together daily, while another asks whether that combination would be a problem, answered with the view that both are low [1].
claims.experts: No sources reviewed address combining oral isotretinoin with a topical retinoid; isotretinoin is prescription-only and prescribers manage its regimen [2].
